cim_eredeti: A look at Jeff Bezos' AI startup Prometheus, which raised $18B and employs ~250 people; sources say it is building an end-to-end agentic AI engineering system (Rebecca Heilweil/Fast Company)
szoveg_eredeti:
For many in the tech industry, physical AI is the next world to conquer. While developers of large language models like OpenAI and Anthropic seek to push reasoning models distilled on billions of streams of text to their limits, an emerging crop of companies are focusing on an even more ambitious goal: developing AI programs designed to speak the language of physics. Should they succeed, these firms have a stake in everything from building models that might power self-driving manufacturing or enable drug discovery to those that can take on plane design and weapons development.

The promise is enormous. Whoever cracks physical AI could control a slice of the software stack that becomes critical to a host of industries—and worth many, many billions. Already, a growing list of companies are racing to stake their claim. Among the buzziest is Prometheus, a startup backed by Jeff Bezos that’s already flush with cash.

Bezos isn’t just bankrolling Prometheus. He’s also coleading the company, marking his first executive role since stepping down as Amazon’s CEO in 2021. His cofounder is Vik Bajaj, a Stanford professor who previously led science operations at Verily, Alphabet’s health technology venture. Prometheus was incubated in 2024 at Foresite Labs, which Bajaj led, with support from the venture capital firm Arch Venture Partners. A number of Prometheus employees also appear to have come from firms associated with Bajaj.

By combing through LinkedIn and researchers’ personal websites, Fast Company identified 130 people who say they’re currently working for Prometheus, and assembled what appears to be the first public database of its kind. Prometheus employs approximately 250 people, including numerous accomplished AI researchers, some of whose names have not been publicly disclosed. The company is recruiting not only AI model developers but also experts in fields like aerospace and chemistry, a strong hint that it may one day target manufacturing and healthcare customers. Employees bring expertise in ocean engineering, energy engineering, mathematics, and even high-performance computing.

In this Subscriber Exclusive, you’ll discover:

At a Semafor event on November 17, Bezos and Bajaj said they’ve spent much of their funding on compute and have built one single multi-physics model. Thus far, Prometheus has built a neural surrogate for numerical simulation and has used the technology to design a range of hardware, including an experiment that involved having the company’s models redesign the Mars helicopter.

This next AI revolution needs AI tools trained not on text but on data from the physical world, as well as subject-matter experts who can ensure that models are distilling a common core of engineering principles that can extend across myriad domains. This, in turn, involves recruiting not just AI coders but plenty of people with expertise in the physical realm, whether that’s manufacturing automotive parts or running biology labs.

“Most fundamentally, the biggest challenge is just the sheer breadth of what we’re doing. Engineering is vast. There’s no such thing as an engineer,” one leading AI expert and early-stage Prometheus employee, speaking on the condition of anonymity, tells Fast Company. “This idea of building something that’s general enough to cover all of that space, that’s been a really, really huge challenge—and a really interesting one.”

News that Prometheus (formerly called the Prometheus Project) was under development went public only last year, and its leadership has been tight-lipped about what it’s actually trying to build. We do know that the company was incubated at Foresite Labs, which is housed within the health and life sciences investment firm Foresite Capital. (In addition to Prometheus, Foresite Labs has backed companies like AI drug discovery startup Xaira and disease therapy outfit Alumis.)

Still, Prometheus’s bare-bones website includes only links to its LinkedIn and X pages, and government documents show that Prometheus used a code name (“FL2024-008 INC”) for a small amount of lobbying and when applying for H1-B visas for some employees.

We also know that Prometheus has attracted significant capital from investors interested in healthcare, AI, and tech manufacturing. The company originally raised about $6 billion in funding, and then another $12 billion—for a $41 billion valuation—earlier this year. Its backers, Semafor reported in June, include JPMorgan; BlackRock; and Arch Venture Partners. Other backers include Powerlaw, a closed-end fund that has also invested in high-tech companies like SpaceX, Colossal, and Waymo, as well as RoboStrategy, a venture capital fund that says it owns shares in the company.

Bezos has said that the company isn’t focused on robotics, though that’s what many people first associate with the term physical AI. Instead, Prometheus aims to develop what it calls an artificial general engineer, which Bezos likens to a much more advanced version of computer-aided design, or CAD, powered by artificial intelligence.

“My through line for the last few years has been AI,” Bezos said in an interview with Squawk Box anchor Andrew Ross Sorkin earlier this year. “My time at Amazon is spent on AI. My time at Prometheus is spent on AI—Prometheus is really an AI company. And my time at Blue [Origin] is largely spent on AI. And [at] Prometheus . . . the tools that we’re building are going to help companies like Blue immensely.”

A trademark application makes clear that Prometheus’s aspirations extend far beyond healthcare, spanning much of the engineering and manufacturing pipeline. The document references physical simulations and digital twin technology, along with structural, thermal, fluid, acoustic, and electromagnetic analysis, and even “acoustic and vibration analysis, noise prediction, and acoustic design optimization.” The application also discusses 3D printing, semiconductor manufacturing, and developing factory layouts.

It’s not hard to see why this interdisciplinary approach might one day prove lucrative. Companies spend an extraordinary amount of time researching and developing new components and hardware, a process that can involve the arduous work of finding and vetting suppliers. There’s also the expensive, resource-intensive process of simulating and testing how new systems perform once they’re built and under different conditions. Another challenge: developing production lines capable of manufacturing that hardware at scale.

Consider the development of a jet engine, a process that can require thousands of workers and more than a decade of design, prototyping, testing, and manufacturing. Prometheus envisions AI tools that could dramatically compress that timeline, from, say, a decade to just a few years. The company sees similar opportunities across everything from household products to large-scale industrial systems.

The aspiration for the physical AI industry is to automate as much of the process as possible and make real-world testing and evaluation far more efficient. The idea is that this could speed up hardware development across a wide range of industries. Indeed, Prometheus reportedly already has its eyes on a network of spin-offs in which it might one day own stakes.

“Today it takes days to weeks for engineers to set up one simulation for one design. There are a lot of repetitive, manual, low-added-value tasks that they have to go through while using this software,” explains Thomas von Tschammer, cofounder of Neural Concept, a physical AI startup and Prometheus competitor. “The opportunity with AI is first of all to automate and compress a lot of this low-added-value work from those engineers so that they can actually spend time engineering.”

lead: A 41 milliárd dollárra értékelt Prometheus a fizikai világ törvényeit értő mesterséges intelligenciával váltaná ki a mérnöki és gyártási folyamatokat.
osszefoglalo:
Jeff Bezos korábbi Amazon-vezérigazgató és Vik Bajaj, a Stanford professzora közösen vezetik a [Prometheus](https://www.prometheus.ai/) nevű AI-startupot. A mintegy 250 alkalmazottat foglalkoztató cég eddig **18 milliárd dollár kockázati tőkét** gyűjtött össze, piaci értékét pedig 41 milliárd dollárra becsülik. A fejlesztőcsapatban a modellépítők mellett repülőgépmérnökök, kémikusok, óceánmérnökök és számítástechnikai szakemberek is dolgoznak.

A vállalat nem a hagyományos szöveges modellekre vagy a robotikára összpontosít, hanem egy úgynevezett **általános mesterséges mérnök rendszert** fejleszt. Ez a megoldás az AI-alapú számítógéppel segített tervezés (CAD) és a fizikai szimulációk összekapcsolásával működik: a rendszert áramlástani, hőtechnikai, akusztikai és elektromágneses szimulációkra képezik ki. A modell segítségével a cég már sikerrel tervezte újra a Mars-helikopter kísérleti változatát.

A Prometheus célja, hogy a komplex ipari alkatrészek, sugárhajtóművek vagy félvezetők többéves tervezési, tesztelési és gyártósor-tervezési ciklusát **néhány évre vagy hétre rövidítse**. Az eljárás automatizálja a mérnökök manuális feladatait, ezáltal felgyorsítja a hardverfejlesztést a hajtóműgyártástól a gyógyszerkutatásig.
miert_szamit: A fizikai modellezést automatizáló AI-eszközök radikálisan **lecsökkentik a hardver- és termékfejlesztési időt**, ami a fizikai termékeket gyártó cégeknek jelentős versenyelőnyt és költségmegtakarítást hozhat.
